subtype: Approach: working backward from months of cash left [Thinking]
passage: Gurpreet had savings for nine months. On the wall of the rented room in Pune he drew a line: last salary in March, savings run out in December. Then he counted backward. To raise money he would need proof by September, which meant a paying customer by August, which meant a working prototype by June. Gurleen, sitting cross-legged with the laptop, asked, "And the logo?" "Does the logo help us get a paying customer by August?" "No." "Then not now." Every task got the same test: does this help prove something by September? The list on the wall shrank from twenty-two items to seven. It felt frightening and calm at the same time.

qa.a: Gurpreet had savings for nine months.

qa.q: What does "frightening and calm at the same time" suggest about how Gurpreet feels?
qa.a: It suggests Gurpreet feels fear of the deadline but also comfort from having a clear plan.

qa.q: What else could Gurpreet do to keep to the timeline?
qa.a: Gurpreet could check progress against the dates every week and speak to possible customers early.

qa.q: How might Gurleen see the logo question and the answer?
qa.a: Gurleen may see it as a fair test that cuts distractions, and accepts putting the logo aside.

grounding: Gurpreet counts back from the last salary date to work out what must be proven by month six and judges every task against that date.

subtype: Approach: working backward from months of cash left [Thinking]
passage:
"Nine months," Rajni said, tapping the whiteboard in their tiny co-working cabin. "It's March. That's all our savings cover, Sachin. The money runs out in November."
"So we have till November."
"No. Think backwards. If we need to raise money before November, investors take about three months to say yes. So by month six, August, we have to show them something real."
"Like what?"
"Like fifty schools paying for the attendance tool. Not using it free. Paying."
Sachin looked at their task list. "Then the new logo..."
"Doesn't get us fifty schools by August."
"Dark mode?"
"Doesn't either."
"Calling the principals I met at the conference?"
"That does. Top of the list."
Sachin crossed out half the list. "This is brutal."
"It's August," Rajni said. "Everything gets measured against August now."

qa.q: By when must they have fifty schools paying?
What does Sachin mean by "This is brutal"?
qa.a: Sachin feels a sting of disappointment at crossing out favourite tasks like the logo, but accepts the reasoning.

qa.q: What else could Rajni and Sachin do to test the August goal early?
qa.a: They could set a smaller checkpoint for May or June, such as ten paying schools, to see if they are on track.

qa.q: How might the principals Sachin met see the calls?
qa.a: The principals may welcome them if the tool solves a real attendance problem, and their answers will quickly show whether schools will pay.

grounding: It shows founders with nine months of savings counting back from the last month and fixing what must be proven by month six, then judging every task against that date.

subtype: Approach: working backward from months of cash left [Thinking]
passage:
When I left my job to build a tuition-booking app, I had exactly nine months of savings. For the first two weeks I worked as if I had forever: fonts, a mascot, a pitch deck with animations.
Then one Sunday Urmila, who had agreed to be my co-founder, drew a line on a napkin. "Eshaan, month nine, you're broke. Raising money takes three months. So month six is the real deadline. What has to be true by month six for someone to invest?"
We argued, then agreed: two hundred parents who have booked and paid for a tutor at least twice. That was the proof.
After that, every task had to answer one question: does this get us closer to two hundred repeat bookings by month six? The mascot went. The animations went. Visits to three coaching centres got added. It felt harsh. It also felt like the first time I knew what I was doing.

qa.q: What proof did they agree on for month six?
qa.a: Two hundred parents who have booked and paid for a tutor at least twice.

qa.q: How did Eshaan feel once every task was judged against month six?
qa.a: It felt harsh, but Eshaan also felt clear and confident for the first time.

qa.q: What could Eshaan add to track progress toward the target?
qa.a: A simple weekly count of repeat bookings, so they can see early if month six is slipping.

qa.q: How does Urmila see the early weeks of fonts and a mascot?
qa.a: Urmila sees them as time spent as if there were no deadline, which is why the line went onto the napkin.

grounding: It shows a founder with nine months of savings working back to what must be proven by month six and judging every task against that date.
